questions.question: Distinguish the physical causes of flooding from the human causes, giving South African examples of each.
questions.expected_answer: Physical causes concern the rain and the catchment. Rainfall intensity matters more than total — fifty millimetres in an hour overwhelms infiltration where the same amount over a week soaks in — and South Africa's summer thunderstorms deliver exactly such bursts. Prolonged rain from a cut-off low, a pocket of cold air that breaks from the upper westerlies and stalls over a region for days, caused both the Laingsburg flood of 1981 and the KwaZulu-Natal floods of April 2022; tropical cyclones such as Eline and Idai drench the north-east. Catchment factors decide the response: antecedent moisture, since a saturated catchment turns nearly all further rain into runoff; steep slopes speeding water into channels; impermeable rock and thin or baked soils; sparse vegetation, removing interception and infiltration; and compact round catchments that deliver all their water to one point at once. Human causes: urbanisation seals the ground with tar, roofs and paving while stormwater drains deliver runoff at speed; deforestation and overgrazing strip vegetation and feed eroded silt into channels and dams, raising beds and shrinking capacity; wetland destruction removes the natural sponges that store and slowly release floodwater; blocked or undersized drains and poorly maintained infrastructure worsen events; and settlement on floodplains — both formal building on cheap flat land and informal settlement on the flood-prone land left to the poorest — places people where the river periodically returns, so that flood risk in South Africa is distributed by inequality.

questions.question: Describe the flood hydrograph in words — its axes and every labelled part — and explain how lag time is defined and why the falling limb is gentler than the rising limb.
questions.expected_answer: A flood hydrograph plots time in hours or days on the horizontal axis against river discharge on the vertical axis, measured in cubic metres per second — cumecs — with the storm's rainfall shown as a block of bars near the start. Before the storm the line runs low and level at base flow, the river's everyday water fed by groundwater seeping into the channel. After the rain begins, the rising limb climbs steeply as fast surface runoff arrives, up to peak discharge, the maximum flow and the moment of greatest flood danger. Lag time is the interval between the heaviest rainfall and peak discharge — defined peak to peak — and represents the travel time water needs to move from where it fell, across slopes and down tributaries, to the measuring station; a short lag means a dangerous river because the flood arrives before warnings can. The falling or recession limb then descends more gently than the rising limb climbed, because the last water arrives by slower routes — throughflow moving laterally in the soil and inflow from the furthest corners of the catchment — before the curve settles onto a base flow slightly higher than before the storm, since the recharged soil now feeds the channel more generously. Interpretation rests on three readings: how high the peak, how short the lag, and how steep the limbs — high, short and steep marking a flashy, dangerous catchment.

questions.question: Compare the hydrographs of an urbanised and a rural vegetated catchment in the same storm, and use the Laingsburg 1981 and eThekwini April 2022 floods to distinguish flash floods from regional floods.
questions.expected_answer: In the same storm, a rural vegetated catchment produces a long lag time because interception and infiltration delay the water; a low, broad peak because much of the rain soaks in and arrives slowly through the soil; gentle limbs; and a persistent base flow between storms because recharged groundwater keeps feeding the channel — the catchment behaves like a sponge. The urbanised catchment produces a short lag because sealed surfaces reject infiltration and stormwater drains deliver water at engineered speed; a high, narrow peak as the same water is compressed into fewer hours; steep rising and falling limbs; and meagre base flow because little water enters the ground — the catchment sheds the storm like a corrugated roof. Urbanisation moves the peak up, the lag down and the limbs toward vertical. Laingsburg, January 1981, was a flash flood: a cut-off low delivered more than 400 millimetres in about two days onto bare, rocky Karoo catchments of the Buffels River; with almost no lag, a wall of water struck the town, much of which stood on the floodplain at a river junction, and 104 people died. eThekwini, April 2022, was a regional flood: days of sustained rain — over 300 millimetres in a day in places — fell on ground already saturated, bringing rivers up across the whole metro for days; more than 400 people died, overwhelmingly in informal settlements on steep slopes and low riverside land, while roads, bridges, water and power failed across the province. Management follows from the hydrograph: lengthen lag and lower peak by restoring wetlands and vegetation, using permeable surfaces, keeping settlement off floodplains, maintaining drains and building early-warning systems.
